extracted.intended_audience: aspiring comics writers, students of storytelling, and fans of Alan Moore
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for writing comics and graphic novels (story, character, worldbuilding, panel-level pacing), distilled from Alan Moore's essay and reader commentary. Useful for creators developing scripts and narrative technique in the comics medium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide on the main idea before you write
rubrics_metrics.description: “Decide on the main idea before you write your story, and save the plot for later.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moore (as summarized) recommends finding the core idea or dramatic premise first — often a 'What if?' — that will engage the reader's mind. The idea can be very brief (even a few words) and need not contain plot details; the plot's job is to serve that central idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot should serve and enhance the story
rubrics_metrics.description: “The purpose of a plot is to enhance your story.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat plot as instrumental: use plot events to illuminate the central idea and character, not as an end in itself. Avoid allowing plot mechanics to overwhelm theme or character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four‑dimensional worldbuilding
rubrics_metrics.description: “Have a clear picture of what your world looks like in four dimensions: What does it look like in the past, present, and future?”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop the setting's history and potential future as well as the present moment so the world feels coherent and lived-in; even if only glimpsed on the page, that temporal depth informs character choices and story logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write for humanity, not the 'average reader'
rubrics_metrics.description: “Get rid of the general belief of your 'average reader'. You don't have to write a story to satisfy your 'average' readers. Instead of thinking about public acceptance, use humanity as the common denominator.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid tailoring work to an imagined generic audience. Aim for truths and emotional resonances that connect to human experience broadly rather than trying to satisfy a nebulous 'average' consumer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Horror should come from your own fears
rubrics_metrics.description: “First think about what sort of things horrify you. Analyze your own fears thoroughly enough and you might be able to reach some conclusions about the broad mass of human fear and anxiety. Be ruthless about this, and submit yourself to as much emotional pain as necessary to get the question answered: What horrifies me?”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For horror writing, mine personal anxieties and interrogate why they affect you — emotional honesty and self-examination produce material that resonates as genuinely horrifying because it reveals what it implies about you and humanity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deep immersion and understanding of subject
rubrics_metrics.description: “If you want to write about something, then you must know it must understand it as fully as possible. Must love it, even if it is unlovable... Immerse yourself in the least desirable element and swim.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research and empathic immersion: to write convincingly about a milieu or group (even unpleasant ones), experience or deeply study it so your portrayal is informed, specific, and humane rather than stereotyped.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid creative comfort: take risks and change
rubrics_metrics.description: “When a writer becomes comfortable, it erodes creativity. It therefore behooves the writer to become uncomfortable, change genre, technique, or style, sometimes all three.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actively force yourself into challenging situations (new forms, genres, techniques) to prevent repetition and stagnation; deliberate risk-taking keeps work vital and prevents becoming 'samey'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create multi‑dimensional characters (avoid 15‑word summaries)
rubrics_metrics.description: Moore criticizes the dictum 'If a character can't be summed up in 15 words then the character is no good.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist reducing characters to single-line summaries. Allow complexity, contradiction, and development rather than insisting every character be instantly encapsulable in a pithy tagline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain panel-to-panel clarity and momentum
rubrics_metrics.description: Advice on comics craft: 'how not to let the reader's interest drop between panels' and 'how to correctly set the dynamics'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On the micro level of comics scripting, ensure transitions between panels preserve narrative momentum and reader comprehension; manage pacing, focus, and visual rhythm so interest never lags between beats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit comics-specific storytelling (not cinema or prose)
rubrics_metrics.description: Moore emphasizes comics as its own creative medium distinct from cinema or literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the unique affordances of comics (panel sequence, interplay of image and text, page architecture, timing) rather than trying to simply emulate film cuts or prose description; design storytelling techniques that only comics can accomplish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be intentional and know the 'why' of your choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Moore 'encourages you, every step of the way, to think about what is right for you and your comic, and why.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make conscious creative decisions: understand motives behind plot points, character actions, visual beats, and stylistic choices rather than relying on habit or imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Script specificity as one viable method
rubrics_metrics.description: Moore's scripts are 'frighteningly thorough and specific in his description of each panel.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed panel-by-panel scripting (specific camera, action, and staging directions) is a valid approach — especially for collaborating with artists — but is a stylistic choice and not the only method. Authors should choose a level of specificity appropriate to their collaborators and goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate characters with textured environments
rubrics_metrics.description: Praise for Moore's 'weaving textures into his character's landscapes' and worldbuilding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embed character psychology and theme into the physical and social environment; use setting detail to enrich character and to create resonant, textured scenes rather than flat backgrounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor character-driven work over plot-dependence
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers note 'dangers of depending too much on [plot]' and a shift toward character-driven stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let character choices and development drive narrative momentum; avoid constructing stories that exist only to showcase plot twists without emotional or thematic payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let idea determine story length and form
rubrics_metrics.description: “There is no limit on how long your story - it can be fifteen words or a few sentences.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose form and length to suit the central idea — brevity or expansiveness is justified by what the idea requires, not by arbitrary market expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use abstract visions and incremental development
rubrics_metrics.description: Moore discusses 'mental steps' and that you 'don't have to begin with a complete view of the story - it can be an abstract thought or a vision.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow the story to grow from an initial abstraction or feeling; develop details iteratively rather than forcing complete answers at the outset. Trust mental/processual steps to form coherent narrative over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study scripts alongside finished comics
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommendation to 'read some of his scripts, alongside their corresponding books' to learn how scripts map to final work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learning method: compare draft scripts to the published pages to see how descriptions translate into art and pacing, helping you calibrate your own scripting style and collaboration expectations.
